notes.meaning: Paul calls himself an apostle, a messenger sent directly by Christ. He says this came about by God's will, not by his own worth or strength. He calls Timothy "our brother" and not his son, a humble way of treating a younger worker as an equal. Timothy had traveled with Paul through this region, so the church would likely have known him.

"Saints" means people set apart for God. "Faithful brothers" points to their bond with fellow believers. Paul wishes them grace, which is God's free kindness, and peace, the good things that flow from it. Colossae was a town in Phrygia, in what is now Turkey.

Paul's prayers for them are full of thanks. Thanksgiving should be part of every prayer, and anything that makes us glad should make us grateful to God. He thanks God as the Father of Jesus. It is through Christ that God becomes our Father too.

Paul had heard from Epaphras about their faith in Christ and their love for all believers. He thanks God for both, because faith and love are God's gifts. Christians owe a special love to fellow believers, even when they differ on smaller points.

Their faith and love spring from hope. Here "hope" means the thing hoped for: the joy of heaven, kept safe for them like treasure no enemy can steal. The more we fix our hope on heaven, the freer we are to do good with what we have now. They first heard of this hope in the gospel, the good news about Jesus, which is true and safe to trust.

Paul pictures the gospel as a living plant spreading across the Roman world. It bears fruit in changed lives and keeps growing as more people believe. The same has been true in Colossae since the day they heard it and truly grasped God's grace. Everyone who hears the gospel should bear its fruit by obeying it.

Epaphras had taught them the gospel. Paul calls him a dear fellow servant and a faithful minister of Christ. This warm praise puts Paul's stamp of approval on what Epaphras taught, so the church would hold to it and not turn to false teachers.

Epaphras told Paul about their "love in the Spirit." This is love the Holy Spirit worked in their hearts, not just natural liking. Such love is holy and not selfish. Faithful ministers are glad to speak well of their people.

Hearing good news about them made Paul pray all the more. He asks that they be filled with knowing God's will. He means knowledge that is lived out, not just facts in the head. Wisdom is knowing how to apply it, and this spiritual understanding comes only as the Spirit guides us through God's word.

Knowing God's will has a purpose: to "walk," or live, in a way worthy of the Lord and pleasing to Him in everything. That means doing every kind of good work, not just the easy ones, and growing in knowing God. Good words will not do without good works.

Paul prays that God's own glorious power would strengthen them, since our own strength is not enough. This strength is mainly for hard times. It gives endurance, which is holding up under trouble, and patience, which is putting up with people without hitting back. Both come with joy, which we could never manage on our own.

Paul calls for thanks to the Father, who has made believers fit to share in the inheritance of God's people in the kingdom of light. No one makes himself fit for heaven by his own merit. God does it. The picture recalls how Israel's promised land was divided into shares for each family.

God has rescued believers from the power of darkness, meaning sin, error and Satan's rule. He has moved them, the way a whole people might be moved to a new country, into the kingdom of His beloved Son. Slaves of Satan become willing subjects of Christ. No change in a person's life matters more.

In Christ we have redemption, which means being set free by a price paid, like buying a slave's freedom. Paul explains that this freedom is the forgiveness of sins. The price was Christ's own blood, his death on the cross. Some older copies leave out "through his blood" here, but the same words stand in Ephesians 1:7.

Jesus is the exact image of the God no one can see. Whoever has seen him has seen the Father. "Firstborn" does not mean Jesus was the first thing created. It means he was there before all creation and holds the highest rank over it, like an eldest son who is heir of everything.

Everything was created in Christ, through him and for him: things in heaven and on earth, things seen and unseen. That includes every rank of angels, here called thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities. So Christ is not a creature but the Creator, and all things exist for his glory. Paul names the angels to show how far above them Christ is, against teachers who wanted people to worship angels.
Christ existed before anything else, which means he is eternal. He also holds everything together. Without his power the universe would fall apart. Only God could do this.

Christ is head of the church, his body. He rules it, and all its life and strength flow from him. He is the "firstborn from the dead," the first to rise never to die again, and his rising is the promise that his people will rise too. So in everything he holds first place.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that, under Christ, the Pope serves as a visible "ministerial" head of the church on earth.

notes.meaning: God was pleased to have all His fullness, everything God is, live in Christ as in a temple. False teachers spread God's powers out among angelic beings. Paul says it all dwells in Christ alone. From that fullness believers receive everything they need.

Through Christ, God makes peace and brings things back into friendship with Himself. He did this through the blood Jesus shed on the cross. This does not mean everyone is actually brought back. Fallen angels are left out, and many people refuse. Teachers explain "things in heaven" in different ways: angels kept secure by Christ, or believers who died before he came.

Once the Colossians were strangers to God and enemies in their thinking. Their wicked deeds showed what was in their hearts. The turning away was not just in one part of them but in their whole mind. All people are the same by nature.

Now Christ has brought them back to God by dying in a real human body. Angels have no such body, so they cannot do this. The goal is to present believers before God holy, spotless and with no charge left against them. Forgiveness and a new, holy life go together.

differ.view: God fills believers with His Spirit and love so they can be made holy and blameless in this life, ready for the judgment.
This holiness is only begun now and grows daily. It is made complete only when Christ returns.

notes.meaning: All this holds if they keep going in the faith. They should stand firm like a building on a solid foundation, not pushed away from the gospel's hope by false teachers. This gospel had been preached far and wide across the world, as Christ commanded. Paul is its servant.

differ.view: Those who do not keep going in the faith will lose the blessings they have already begun to enjoy.
This is a call to keep going. True faith is firm and settled enough to withstand every attack, so believers need not live in doubt about whether they will last.

notes.meaning: Paul is glad to suffer for them. "What is lacking" does not mean Christ's suffering to save us was not enough; that was perfect and complete. Christ's people are his body, and he shares in their troubles. The church has its share of suffering to carry, and Paul is bearing his part for the good of the whole church.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching has linked this verse to the idea that the sufferings of the saints, joined with Christ's, form a "treasury" the church can draw on when granting indulgences, which are releases from punishment due for sin.

notes.meaning: Paul became the church's servant through a job God trusted to him, like a household manager. He did not take it for himself. His task was to preach God's word fully, especially to the Gentiles, meaning people who are not Jewish.
A "mystery" in the Bible is a secret God once kept hidden but has now made known openly. It was hidden through the ages before Christ. Now God has shown it to His people, first through the apostles.

The secret is that Gentiles share fully in God's rich and glorious blessings. It is summed up in "Christ in you, the hope of glory." Christ living in believers' hearts now is their sure hope of heaven's glory to come. This was all God's free choice, not something anyone earned.

Paul and his helpers proclaim Christ. They warn people about how they live and teach them what to believe, with all wisdom. Their goal is to present every single person mature and complete in Christ when he comes. No one is left out, and every soul matters.

Paul works hard for this goal and strains like an athlete in a contest. He does it not in his own strength but by God's mighty power at work in him. The more we work for the Lord, the more help we may expect from Him.
